extracted.intended_audience: research council staff, science policy researchers, scientometricians, and research-evaluation practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Case-study criteria and metrics for evaluating grant applications and the allocation process (peer review vs bibliometrics) in the social and behavioral sciences; includes operationalizations, statistical tests, and policy-relevant conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past performance — publications (3-year window)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of publications by the applicant in the three years prior to the application (publication years as indicated on the publications), measured from the Social Science Citation Index (SoSCI).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an operationalization of past performance; chosen 3-year window because the application form lists recent publications. Caveats: books and other non-journal outputs are not counted (serious disadvantage in fields such as law), SoSCI coverage varies across subfields, publication-year dating issues, and the measure may require field-specific interpretation. Publication counts were highly skewed; statistical analyses should account for skew (e.g., use nonparametric statistics or stratification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Past performance — citations (to those publications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of citations received by the applicant's publications in the specified 3-year window (times cited measured at a fixed date: 9 Feb 2007 in this study).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations correlate strongly with publications (ρ ≈ 0.92) and were given priority in some predictive analyses. Caveats: citation windows are disputed in social sciences; citation meaning (quality vs visibility) is unclear; citation practices differ between disciplines; distributions are skewed; name-matching errors affect counts. Interpret with caution and by discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review / referee scores (proposal quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees' assessments of the proposal, operationalized by the Council's referee scores (translated into a unified five-point scale where 1 = excellent and 5 = poor). Referee judgments are taken as the measure of proposal quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referee scores correlate moderately with funding received (ρ ≈ 0.46 in the whole sample) and improve predictive classification when combined with bibliometrics. But peer review has known problems: reviewer inconsistency, possible gender bias and nepotism, committee-level compromises, and different formats (individual reviews vs committee reviews). Different programs use different review steps (e.g., replies, presentations) that affect outcomes. Statistical treatment should account for scale inversion and skew; local context (Dutch conventions where '3' is considered low) matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of applicant's network (co-applicants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operationalized as average network quality (average publications and citations for applicant and co-applicants) and maximal network quality (highest publications/citations among applicant and co-applicants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to capture the influence of co-applicants; applicable mainly to open-competition applications (career grants typically have no co-applicants). Findings: co-applicant quality positively influences success but effect is weak. Authors note other possible network measures (PhD supervisor status, co-author networks) that were not included but may matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding instrument and selection procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of application by funding instrument (OC open competition; Veni, Vidi, Vici career programs) and associated procedural differences (pre-selection, review, invitation to presentation, committee decision rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The role of past performance and the weight of different evidence vary by instrument; analyses should be stratified by instrument because selection criteria and procedures differ. Example: Veni preselection and presentations affect decision mechanics; small N in some instruments (e.g., Vici) may limit inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline-specific publication and citation norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that disciplines differ in publication types, citation rates, typical journal impact factors, and SoSCI coverage (e.g., psychology vs sociology vs law).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bibliometric indicators and referee behavior must be interpreted by discipline. Use discipline-level analyses because aggregated results can mask field-specific patterns. For fields where books are central, journal-based bibliometrics seriously undercount performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of bibliometric indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: The constraints and potential biases of using bibliometric measures (SoSCI coverage gaps, English-language bias, differing citation patterns across fields, incomplete coverage of publication types, and name-matching errors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bibliometrics can be institutionalized and useful for screening (especially to remove the low-performing tail), but are less reliable at the level of individual researchers or for interdisciplinary fields. Beware perverse incentives (gaming behavior), and consider combining bibliometrics with peer review rather than using bibliometrics alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundability/outcome categories and funding amount
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision variable operationalization: three-category fundability status ('A' = fundable and funded; 'A-' = fundable but not funded; 'B' = non-fundable) and actual euros awarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses were run both on categorical fundability (A / A- / B) and on funding amount. Choice of dependent variable affects statistical approach (classification vs amount regression). Use both when possible to understand both selection and allocation of funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical evaluation and predictive validity (ANOVA, Spearman's rho, Discriminant Analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of statistical tests to evaluate differences and predictive relationships: ANOVA to compare groups, Spearman's rho for associations (appropriate for skewed data), and discriminant analysis (DA) for classification of successful vs unsuccessful applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distributions of bibliometric measures are skewed—use nonparametric or robust methods (Spearman's rho) and be cautious with DA assumptions. Stratification (e.g., selecting top unsuccessful applicants) can radically change results. In this study DA with publications and citations alone predicted only a small fraction of successful cases; adding referee scores improves classification markedly, but much variance remains unexplained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness at discarding the tail versus selecting the top
rubrics_metrics.description: The system's ability to remove the low-performing tail of applicants versus its (lack of) ability to distinguish among top-performing applicants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical result: councils successfully discard low performers (the tail) but do not reliably pick the 'best' among above-average applicants; top-performing rejected applicants often outperformed funded ones on bibliometric measures and referee scores. Policy implication: selection procedures may be better framed as screening rather than fine-grained selection among elite candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender bias correction and equity adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration and explicit correction for gender effects in selection (the Council under study applied a positive correction for gender).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gender bias has historical evidence; meta-analyses confirm diminishing but existing bias. Corrections can and were implemented; evaluators should track gender effects, apply corrections if policy dictates, and monitor outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary research assessment challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that interdisciplinary research tends to receive lower grades in peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referee panels and bibliometrics may undervalue interdisciplinary proposals; special procedures or evaluation criteria may be needed to avoid bias against interdisciplinary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee decision dynamics and strategic behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Committee review process often involves members assessing a subset of applications but deciding on all, producing compromises and strategic behavior (e.g., members ensuring funding for favored proposals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These social processes can bias outcomes. Recommendations include regularly rotating committees/panels, evaluating potential biases, and increasing reflexivity in procedures to maintain openness and reduce entrenched networks' influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation quality criteria: reliability, validity, fairness/justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of evaluation systems using technical criteria such as reliability, validity, and justice—used in previous studies of selection systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review can be adequate on average regarding these criteria but still produces Type I and II errors. Evaluation of selection procedures should report on these dimensions and quantify error rates where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use bibliometrics as technocratic screening, not sole innovation criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to use bibliometric indicators to discard the low-performing tail while recognizing they are conservative and not necessarily aligned with stimulating innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the goal is to stimulate innovation, bibliometric screening may be counterproductive; combining methods and maintaining diversity of funding instruments is advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational coding of heterogeneous referee scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Mapping heterogeneous referee-scoring schemes into a single comparable scale (the study translated varying 3- and 5-point scales into a unified five-point scale; Table 1 shows coding conventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When panels/instruments use different scoring systems, create an explicit mapping and document local interpretation (e.g., Dutch context where a score of 3 is considered low). Be transparent about recoding rules and implications for analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data quality: name-matching and measurement error
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical data-quality issue where author names in bibliographic databases can be inconsistently recorded (e.g., initials), producing matching errors between application records and bibliometric data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge and, where feasible, correct matching errors; otherwise report margins of error. Small-scale manual checks or disambiguation procedures improve accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to evaluate ex post (post-performance) to assess selection effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the allocation process should include follow-up (post-performance) of funded versus unfunded applicants to judge predictive validity of selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This study did not measure post-performance due to data limits; future studies should track ex post outcomes to assess Type I/II errors and the long-term effectiveness of funding decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stratified sampling and controlling for skew in comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: When comparing funded and unfunded applicants, stratify by instrument and consider top-tail selection because skewed distributions can distort average-based comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors show that comparing funded applicants to the top unsuccessful applicants (stratified by instrument) reverses many apparent correlations. Use stratification to control for instrument mix and long tails before drawing inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual factors influencing allocation (discipline share, institutional distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition that contextual factors — e.g., dominance of psychology in allocations, distribution of funds across disciplines, institutional priorities — influence funding outcomes beyond measured scholarly quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of allocation fairness and effectiveness should include contextual variables (discipline, university, scheme) and consider policy goals (system-level variation, innovation support) when interpreting outcomes.
